newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuelan jail fire started by guards - official.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan jail fire started by guards - official.

text.p: A fire that killed at least 25 inmates at a Venezuelan jail was started by national guardsmen who lobbed incendiary devices and tear gas into an overcrowded cell, officials said on Wednesday.

National Prisons Director Antonio Marval said Tuesday's fire appeared to have been deliberately caused by guards who locked up a group of inmates in a cramped cell at La Planta prison and threw in tear gas and incendiary devices.
"There were tear gas canisters and incendiary devices there," Marval told reporters outside the jail. He did not know why the guards had decided to lock up the inmates.
Prisoners said the fire began after an argument broke out between inmates and prison guards during a roll call. About 40 inmates were trapped inside the locked cell.
"Prisoners say the guards threw in incendiary bombs and, as they were locked in, they could not escape," Congressman Rafael Navaez told reporters.

Defence Minister Nicolas Valencia said on Tuesday he had ordered the arrest of six national guardsmen involved in the incident. The guard provides additional security at Venezuela's overcrowded and violence-prone prisons.

Morgue officials said 25 charred and twisted bodies had been recovered at La Planta prison on the southwestern outskirts of the capital. They said only five had been identified because the bodies were so badly burned.

"What happened here was murder ... There was a mountain of horribly burned bodies one on top of the another because they all died trying to reach a small gap in the roof," the jail's chaplain, Aurelio Ferrin, told Reuters.

A Reuters photographer who entered the burned-out cell on Tuesday said several prisoners had tried to escape the flames by hiding under beds, while others were fused together from clinging to one another as they waited to die.
"I knew them all. It's not fair that they suffered this punishment," said Ferrin. He said many of the dead were accused of minor crimes and most had not been sentenced.

About 100 crying relatives, many of whom had camped out overnight, waited anxiously outside the jail to know if their loved ones were among the dead, turning visiting day into one of mourning and confusion.
"I went to identify my brother but it's impossible. All I saw was coal," said Carmen Luisa Alvarado. Her brother Libio Alvarado spent a year in La Planta awaiting trial for robbery.
"He slept in that room with about 40 people, one on top of the other, but we still don't know if he is alive or not," she sobbed.
Venezuela's overcrowded and decaying prisons, considered to be among the most dangerous in Latin America, are frequent scenes of violence between inmates and clashes with guards.

The tragedy at La Planta was the worst in Venezuela's jails since about 120 prisoners were burned or hacked to death with machetes during a gang fight at the Sabaneta jail in the western city of Maracaibo in January 1994.
La Planta was built for 300 prisoners but currently holds about 1,700, officials said.
